content:
I don't think the puzzle is well-defined under CodinGame's single-answer evaluation system. The issue is that different valid strategies can produce different, yet equally correct, guess sequences.

For example, with 9 prisoners, suppose the first 8 hats contain 4 black and 4 white. A parity-based strategy can be formulated either in terms of black hats or white hats. While these are logically equivalent strategies, they can still lead to different outputs as the last prisoner's guess varies based on the strategy adopted.

As the referee expects a single canonical answer per test case, the puzzle in the current form can't be accepted.

Please correct me if I'm wrong.
The colors of the hats are assigned as described in the problem statement. Black is 1 and white is 0. Thus there can only be 1 correct set of guesses resulting in >= N - 1 prisoners being saved

Assigning black = 1 and white = 0 does not resolve the issue. The ambiguity is not in how the colors are encoded, but in the fact that multiple valid parity strategies exist, each producing a different sequence of guesses while still guaranteeing that at least (N-1) prisoners are saved.

Using Test 1 as an example:

Strategy A: The last prisoner announces the parity of black hats. They guess black (1) if they see an even number of black hats in front of them, and white (0) otherwise.

• Prisoner 3 sees one black hat in front of them (odd), so they guess white (0).
• From Prisoner 3's guess, Prisoner 2 deduces that the total number of black hats among Prisoners 1 and 2 must be odd. Since Prisoner 2 sees one black hat in front of them, they conclude that their own hat is white (0).
• Prisoner 1 can then determine that their hat must be black (1).
• This produces the output [0, 0, 1].

Strategy B: The last prisoner instead announces the parity of white hats. They guess white (0) if they see an even number of white hats in front of them, and black (1) otherwise.

• Prisoner 3 sees one white hat in front of them (odd), so they guess black (1).
• From Prisoner 3's guess, Prisoner 2 deduces that the total number of white hats among Prisoners 1 and 2 must be odd. Since Prisoner 2 sees no white hats in front of them, they conclude that their own hat is white (0).
• Prisoner 1 then determines that their hat must be black (1).
• This produces the output [1, 0, 1].

Both strategies are valid, both satisfy the requirement that at least (N-1) prisoners survive, and both are consistent with the hat assignment in the test case. Therefore, unless the problem explicitly specifies a unique strategy or expected convention, there can be more than one correct output for the same input.

I hope this clarifies my point.
According to google, I can submit a script based evaluator to accept any answer resulting in N - 1 prisoners being saved
Also, the user should be able to try both strategies if they fully understand the problem and submit the 1 resulting in the given solution
Regardless of what Google might tell you, CodinGame does not provide a way for a referee to accept multiple valid outputs for a test case unless the puzzle is created using their SDK.
right, so I can create the puzzle with the SDK then
You can, but in that case the puzzle becomes trivial. A player could simply output the input hat sequence in reverse order and successfully solve every instance.
A script based evaluator could protect against such a solution
Even if the solution is trivial, it's still valid. The evaluator shouldn't disallow such a solution.

The solution should be based on only 1 of the 2 strategies you illustrated above. The evaluator can be scripted to make sure each answer reflects a given strategy as opposed to a reversed input sequence

If you intend to require a specific parity strategy, you can incorporate that as part of the puzzle input, without the need to recreate the puzzle in the SDK. The reason is that once the strategy is fixed, each test case will have a unique expected output, eliminating the ambiguity caused by multiple valid parity conventions.

For broader test coverage, you could include cases that use the "black parity" convention and others that use the "white parity" convention. This would verify that solutions correctly follow the specified strategy rather than relying on an assumed convention.

In addition, if I understand correctly, the referee (SDK or not) evaluates each test case *independently*. As a result, any evaluator you write for an SDK version has no way to verify that a coder is applying the same strategy consistently across all test cases.

The solution must use either "black parity" or "white parity" across all test cases based on the final sentence in the problem description, "Before the game starts, the prisoners can meet to agree on a strategy." The easiest way to make this compliant with the web submission interface would be to introduce a rule stating that before any other prisoner can guess, prisoner N must act as the anchor for the team. Prisoner N's guess is strictly treated as a signaling mechanism. Prisoner N must shout "Black" if they see an odd number of Black hats in front of them or "White" if they see an even number of Black hats in front of them. If Prisoner N's guess does not accurately match the odd/even parity of the hats ahead of them, the entire strategy is disqualified instantly, and all prisoners remain in prison.

What I'm saying is that you don't necessarily need to enforce a single strategy across all test cases. Instead, you can treat each test case pair as an independent scenario, where the prisoners are allowed to agree on whichever strategy is most appropriate before the "game" begins. In other words, the chosen strategy may vary from one test case to another, rather than requiring the same parity convention to be used universally.
